analysis.one_liner: Lets service members sue the federal government for medical malpractice in military hospitals.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill by a 14-12 vote and placed it on the House calendar in April 2010, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: For decades, a Supreme Court ruling known as the Feres Doctrine has barred active-duty service members from suing the government for injuries caused by negligent military medical care. This bill would amend the Federal Tort Claims Act to allow damage claims against the United States for negligent or wrongful medical, dental, or related care provided by government health workers, including care given outside the United States. It would not allow suits over combat activities, and it would not reduce any recovery by the amount of Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance benefits. Claims could reach back to injuries arising on or after January 1, 1997.
analysis.who_benefits: Active-duty service members who are injured, and the families of those killed, by negligent or wrongful medical care in the military health system. Under current law they cannot sue for damages, unlike civilian patients who can sue for malpractice. The bill would open the courthouse door to them, and its effective date would allow claims for injuries going back to 1997.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Federal Tort Claims Act to allow claims for damages for the personal injury or death of a service member arising out of negligent or wrongful medical, dental, or related health care provided by government personnel.

Covers care provided inside or outside the United States; for care abroad, the lawsuit would apply the law of the plaintiff's home state rather than the law of the foreign country where the care occurred.
Prohibits a claim from being reduced by any benefit the family received under Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance, so insurance payouts would not be subtracted from damages.
Excludes claims arising out of combatant activities during armed conflict, limiting the change to medical care rather than battlefield decisions.
Applies to claims arising on or after January 1, 1997, with the clock on older claims starting at enactment, so families with past injuries could file.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government itself pays. Damages judgments in military malpractice cases would come from the Treasury, and the military health system would face lawsuits and litigation costs it is currently shielded from. Taxpayers ultimately bear those costs, though only where negligence is proven.

drawbacks.text: Exposing the government to malpractice suits means the Treasury pays damages judgments and the military health system bears the cost of defending and settling negligence claims, costs that do not exist today because the Feres Doctrine blocks such suits.
The retroactive effective date back to January 1, 1997 could generate a wave of claims for years-old injuries that both sides assumed were closed.

Defenders of the existing rule have long argued that barring suits against the military protects military discipline and keeps courts from second-guessing service decisions; this bill addresses that objection for combat but applies it only to medical care, leaving a narrower version of that argument about defense costs and internal accountability.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: a group of people who today have no legal remedy for proven medical negligence would gain one, and the cost falls on the government that employs the negligent caregivers. That cost is real but bounded by the bill's own limits (no combat claims, no offset by life-insurance benefits), and it is the same liability civilian hospitals already face. The retroactive reach back to 1997 is the least careful part of the design, since it invites claims far older than a typical malpractice window. On balance the benefit to injured service members and their families outweighs the fiscal cost, though the retroactivity provision is debatable.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Judiciary Committee by a 14-12 vote, was reported to the House and placed on its calendar in April 2010, and the House never voted on it before the two-year Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the bill on March 12, 2009, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
The Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law held a hearing in March 2009 and a markup in May 2009, forwarding the bill to the full committee in amended form.
On October 7, 2009, the full Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported in amended form by a narrow 14-12 vote, signaling significant opposition even in committee.
On April 26, 2010, the committee reported the bill with an amendment (H. Rept. 111-466) and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills awaiting House floor action.
The bill never received a vote in the full House and died at the end of the 111th Congress in January 2011.

The reported version was stronger than the original: it extended coverage to negligent care provided outside the United States, while the introduced version covered only care inside the United States.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal government is better off: it avoided opening itself to malpractice suits from service members, and it paid nothing. Service members and their families remain unable to sue for negligent military medical care.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan (10 Democrats, 2 Republicans) and the committee reported it by a narrow 14-12 vote, but the record does not show the party split of that vote, so the partisan shape is unclear.

industries.note: The bill would remove the government's legal shield against malpractice suits by service members, exposing it to damages judgments and litigation costs whenever government health workers cause negligent injury. Its interest in keeping that shield runs directly against injured patients' interest in a remedy.

Doctors and nurses in the military health system would face the same professional negligence liability civilian providers already face. For patients, that exposure is the mechanism of accountability; for providers, it is a new legal risk.
The bill ensures life-insurance benefits are not deducted from malpractice recoveries, so beneficiaries keep the full value of their policies alongside any damages.
